pages.name: Back to the angle
pages.text: Lesson 1 went from an angle to a side. Now run it backwards. The 150 mm offset had 300 mm between its bends, the opposite side and the hypotenuse, so `sin θ = 150 ÷ 300 = 0.5`. Which angle has a sine of 0.5? The `sin⁻¹` key, read [[inverse sine]], answers that: `sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30°`. Like `f⁻¹` in Functions and their graphs, it is the machine run backwards. sin takes 30° to 0.5, and `sin⁻¹` takes 0.5 back to 30°.

pages.name: Opposite and hypotenuse
pages.task: A right-angled triangle has 6 cm opposite `θ` and a 10 cm hypotenuse. What is `θ`?
pages.why: Opposite and hypotenuse make the sine, so `sin θ = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6`. The inverse sine undoes it, `sin⁻¹ 0.6 = 36.9°`. In degrees mode the calculator gives this from `sin⁻¹(6 ÷ 10)`.

pages.name: Which key, and a slope
pages.text: Choose the key from the two sides you have, as you chose the ratio in lesson 1. Opposite and hypotenuse take `sin⁻¹`, adjacent and hypotenuse `cos⁻¹`, opposite and adjacent `tan⁻¹`. A slope's gradient is rise ÷ run, as in Straight-line graphs. The rise is opposite its angle and the run next to it, so the gradient is `tan θ`. Drawn to the same scale on both axes, `y = 0.5x` climbs at `tan⁻¹ 0.5 = 26.6°`.

pages.name: A tray's slope
pages.task: A cable tray rises 1 m over a 2.5 m run, measured level. At what angle does it climb?
pages.why: The rise is opposite the angle and the run is next to it, so they make the tangent. `tan θ = 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.4`, and `tan⁻¹ 0.4 = 21.8°`.

pages.name: Two exact triangles
pages.text: Two triangles give exact ratios with no calculator. Cut a square with sides of 1 from corner to corner. Each half has two sides of 1 and two equal angles that share 90°, so each is 45°. By Pythagoras its hypotenuse is `√2`, so `sin 45° = 1/√2`, which is 0.7071. An equilateral triangle's three equal angles share 180°, so each is 60°. Cut one with sides of 2 down the middle. The top angle splits into two of 30° and the base into two of 1, so the height is `√(4 − 1) = √3`. So `sin 30° = 1/2` and `cos 30° = √3/2`, which is 0.866.

pages.name: cos 60°
pages.task: Use the half equilateral triangle. What is `cos 60°`?
pages.why: At the 60° corner the side next to it is the base, 1, and the hypotenuse is 2. So `cos 60° = 1/2 = 0.5`. It is the same as `sin 30°`, as sin and cos swap between 30° and 60°.

pages.name: An angle or a number
pages.text: On sin, cos and tan, ⁻¹ means undo. In Powers and roots `2⁻¹` meant `1 ÷ 2`, so it is worth saying twice. `sin⁻¹ 0.5` is an angle, 30°. `1 ÷ sin 30°` is a number, 2.0. One over a ratio has a name of its own. `1 ÷ sin θ` is the [[cosecant]], written `cosec θ`, and it is lesson 1's conduit multiplier. The other two of the six ratios are the secant, `sec θ = 1 ÷ cos θ`, and the cotangent, `cot θ = 1 ÷ tan θ`.

pages.name: Shrink
pages.task: Lesson 1's 150 mm offset at 30° has 300 mm of conduit between its bends, but covers less than that along the wall. The difference is the [[shrink]]. What is it?
pages.why: Along the wall the conduit covers only the run, the side next to 30°. The run is `300 × cos 30° = 259.8 mm`, so the shrink is `300 − 259.8 = 40.2 mm`. That is 0.268 for each mm of offset, exactly `2 − √3`. Field tables round it to 3/16 or 1/4 per inch of offset, a field allowance, not a code rule.

pages.name: The arrow and its shadows
pages.text: A force is drawn as an arrow: its length is the size, its tilt the direction. This 100 N arrow stands at 30° above the floor. pages.name: On a slope
pages.text: Tilt the floor into a slope at angle `α` (alpha), and the same split works along the slope and square to it. Its part into the slope is next to `α`, `W cos α`. Its part down the slope is opposite, `W sin α`. For 500 N on 20°: 469.8 N and 171.0 N. Drag the top of the slope.
